name: Talking without internet
desc: Walkie-talkies, news by radio, texts when the network is busy, Morse, notes and a contact plan

guides.w: Talk to your group without a network
s: PMR446 walkie-talkies need no licence and no network anywhere in the EU.
Range: about 1–3 km in town, more in open country or from high ground.
Agree a channel and a backup channel in advance, and write them down.
Agree check-in times (for example every full hour) and switch on only then to save batteries.
Keep messages short: say who you are, the message, then “over”. Only one person can talk at a time.
Keep spare batteries.

guides.w: When internet and TV are down
s: A battery or wind-up radio keeps working when the power and internet are out.
In the Netherlands, the regional broadcaster and NPO Radio 1 give official information in a disaster.
In Italy, RAI radio carries official announcements.
Listen at the top of the hour, when the news is on, to save batteries.
Write down what you hear: times, places, instructions.
d: Don't trust rumours: wait for official information

guides.t: Texts when the network is busy
guides.w: Calls fail but you need to reach someone
s: Send a text instead of calling: it uses much less network and gets through when calls don't.
Keep it short: where you are, if you're OK, what you'll do next.
112 works on any network your phone can find, even without your own provider.
If the network comes and goes, write your message ready and send it when you see a bar of signal.
This app's group also works by text message and Bluetooth when there's no internet.
d: Don't keep calling: it blocks the network for others

s: SOS is · · · — — — · · · (three short, three long, three short). Repeat it with a pause between.
Short = a quick flash or beep; long = three times as long.
A few letters: A ·—  E ·  I ··  O ———  S ···  T —  N —·  H ····
Use a torch, a phone light, a mirror in the sun, or knocking on a pipe.
Three of anything (three whistles, three flashes, three fires) is the international sign for help.
Agree one place where your group leaves notes: a door, a tree, a café, the meeting point.
Write: who, the date and time, where you're going, and when you'll be back or where to meet.
Put it in a plastic bag or bottle if it can get wet.
At home: a note inside a window is visible from outside without being found by everyone.
Chalk on walls or pavements works too: an arrow and the time.
d: Don't write that the house is empty for days

guides.t: A contact plan for your people
guides.w: Make it now, before anything happens
s: Agree two meeting points: one near home and one outside your town, in case you can't get home.
Pick one contact person who lives far away: everyone checks in with them. Long-distance lines often work when local ones are busy.
Write important phone numbers on paper and keep a copy in your wallet: a dead phone has no contacts.
Agree times to switch on phones or walkie-talkies.
Make sure children and older family members know the plan too.
